..(Friday night through Wednesday)
Issued at 250 AM EDT THU OCT 8 2026

The long term period will open with broad mid-level troughing 
over the northeastern CONUS and ridging off the Atlantic Coast; 
this subtropical ridge will expand westward during the day on 
Friday, keeping weather quiet, although with high temperatures 
running above average (ranging from the upper 70s to mid 80s). To 
the south of the forecast area, however, Hurricane Isaias will 
continue to progress northward towards the Gulf Coast, with this 
system being our primary focus this weekend. The current NHC 
forecast suggests that the storm will make landfall as a hurricane
in this region overnight. In a strongly sheared environment, 
Isaias should be rather asymmetric, with the most impactful 
weather on the eastern side of the storm. Then, the storm will 
quickly weaken as it becomes post-tropical.

By Saturday, what remains of Isaias will ride north, owing to 
deep southerly flow along the periphery of the ridge. This track 
will set the remnant low on a collision course with a weaker cut 
off low initially near the TX/LA border. Although this system will
have lost its tropical characteristics by this point, its 
associated surface low should still remain well defined, with a 
large precipitation shield primarily on the eastern side of the 
storm. Increasingly southerly flow aloft should work to increase 
PWs throughout the day, with LREF mean PW values rising to the 
1.2-1.3 inch range by Saturday evening (roughly 70th to 80th 
percentile compared to climatology). LREF guidance indicates that 
the most likely time of rain onset would be late Saturday into 
very early Sunday morning, with the earliest rain chances near the
TN line. However, there is still uncertainty regarding the exact 
track and timing of the original system, and it is worth noting 
that even the 25th percentile LREF suggests rain could easily 
begin as early as Saturday evening. Then, the system looks to take
an eastward turn as it is pushed out by a trough arriving from 
the west, with rain chances finally diminishing gradually Monday 
morning.

A primary hazard with this system will be rainfall, potentially 
heavy at times. WPC has introduced a Marginal Risk (Level 1/4) for
Excessive Rainfall near the I-75 corridor from Saturday morning 
through Sunday morning, corresponding with the highest confidence 
in higher rainfall totals. 

A second hazard will be the potential for gusty winds. Saturday 
evening and overnight, southeasterly winds could become breezy to 
gusty, with strong winds aloft associated with Isaias impacting 
the higher terrain along the TN, VA, and WV borders. Both the GFS 
and ECMWF indicate 50-60 kt winds at 850 mb. 01Z NBM ensemble 
guidance indicates a 30-75% probability of surface wind gusts 
meeting or exceeding 40 mph overnight Saturday into Sunday. 
Ensemble probabilities have increased over the last several model 
runs in both the NBM and LREF ensembles. This trend will continue 
to be closely monitored in subsequent model runs.

Consequently, low level shear will be quite dramatic, with even 
LREF mean 0-1 km SRH in the range of 300-400 m2/s2 as the 
disturbance arrives. Individual deterministic model soundings 
display even higher parameters; however, any tornado risk would 
depend on the timing of the lows arrival and the structure of the 
system itself, particularly with respect to the nature and 
location of any dry air entrainment within the parent low. Thus, 
this remains a very low confidence scenario at present. A
significant mitigating factor will be the cross-barrier mid- and 
low-level flow upstream and any drying/stabilizing effects from 
downsloping off of the Cumberland Mountains. Global models 
typically underestimate this effect at these lead times, with 
high-resolution CAMS likely providing a better handle on any 
mitigating impacts on this risk. 

The system exits east from the area Sunday night into Monday, but
upslope west to southwesterly low-level flow and stronger
northwesterly flow aloft will mean a continued Q-G warm advection
scenario persists into the daytime hours, and thus forcing for 
ascent and sufficient remaining moisture should be able to produce
some light rain lingering into Monday, at least toward the
Cumberland Mountains.

After a brief drying/clearing trend later Monday into early 
Tuesday, a cold front will drop southeast through the Ohio Valley 
and bring the next low chance for rain, mainly east of Interstate 
75. High pressure then brings mild weather for Wednesday along 
with cool nights Tuesday and Wednesday nights.
